questions.question: When is a metric space $(\boldsymbol{X},d)$ called complete?
options: Every sequence contained in it is Cauchy.
No sequence in it converges.
Every point is at distance $1$ from every other point.
Every Cauchy sequence in it converges in $(\boldsymbol{X},d)$.
questions.explanation: A metric space $(X,d)$ is complete when every Cauchy sequence contained in it converges in $(X,d)$. Completeness means no Cauchy sequence has a 'missing' limit.
questions.source_support: The definition states that each Cauchy sequence contained within the space converges in it.

Complete spaces have convergent Cauchy sequences; they do not prevent convergence.
Distance $1$ between all distinct points describes the discrete metric, unrelated to completeness.
